results.summary: This project implements the VLIW processor from the game HOVALAAG, a Zachlike assembly puzzle game. The processor uses 32-bit instructions and 12-bit I/O, which are shifted in and out serially over 10 clocks per processor clock. It can be tested by downloading the game's assembler to generate programs and feeding them through the serial interface. The design is notable for being a hardware implementation of a game CPU, created with permission from the game's author.

This is a simple 4-bit adder designed for educational purposes, originally described in VHDL and ported to Verilog using a ghdl plugin. It takes two 4-bit inputs and produces a 4-bit sum plus a carry-out. The design is intended to be tested with testbenches available in the associated GitHub repository. It is a basic building block useful for teaching digital arithmetic.

This design detects whether a 31-bit number is prime by iteratively dividing it by all smaller numbers. The number is shifted in serially via an SPI-like interface, and the result is indicated by a dedicated pin after computation. It requires an external clock and uses a finite state machine with an iterative divider to minimize area. The design is an experiment in implementing a prime detector on a small scale.

This project multiplies two 8-bit numbers to produce a 16-bit result. The inputs are clocked in one nibble at a time, and the result is clocked out one byte at a time. It includes a synchronous reset and is intended for testing basic multiplication functionality. The design is a straightforward arithmetic unit with a simple serial interface.

This design loads two 4-bit nibbles into registers and transmits the resulting byte over UART. It uses mode pins to select whether the nibble is the least or most significant half of the byte, and a transmit mode to send the data. An Arduino can be used to test the UART output. The design is a simple serial communication interface for sending bytes.

This project implements three pulse-density modulator architectures: PWM, DDPM, and Sigma-Delta, for digital-to-analog conversion. It includes both a 6-bit DC input section and an 8-bit sine wave section to evaluate spectral performance. The outputs are intended to be low-pass filtered to recover the analog signal, and the design is implemented using myHDL and Python. It serves as a comparison of different PDM techniques for DAC applications.

This design performs a 2x2 matrix multiplication on binary matrices, producing a 2x2 result. Each matrix element is a single bit, set via input pins, and the output is provided as four 2-bit values. It is a minimal arithmetic unit that humorously claims to slow down AI model training. The design is purely combinational and requires no external hardware beyond switches and LEDs.

This project is a balanced ternary calculator that supports addition, subtraction, and multiplication with negative numbers. It uses binary-encoded ternary inputs and outputs, with function selection via one of the input pins. The documentation is essentially missing, with only placeholder text for how it works and how to test. It requires no external hardware according to the description.

This design receives two I2S audio streams, mixes them according to a selection input, and transmits the result as an I2S stream. It supports mute, channel 1, channel 2, or a sum of both channels, with the LSB truncated during addition. The design requires an external I2S master to provide clocks and word select signals. It is a simple audio mixer for I2S digital audio.

This project is an attempt to implement a simple FPGA-like counter on TinyTapeout. After reset, a counter increments every second, with the value displayed on a 7-segment display. The documentation is minimal, with only a TODO for how it works. It serves as a basic test of counter functionality and display driving.
